questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Peace and conflict courses not available in UCPH (I'm a pacifist). This is my 2. exchange so I got my 4. priority. Academic and teaching quality at least on par with UCPH/not significantly lower (I looked at all the rankings and student reports I could find while staying inside Erasmus grant eligible destinations).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very good academically, but quite boring housing/city especially during winter time so if possible come here during the Spring semester as I did (don't be discouraged by my experience).

questions.answer: Quite OK, but always a lot of things to get to know.

questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
https://housingoffice.se/
. I lived a few hundred meters from the Government+Peace and Conflict University Department that I would say it could be counted as having been "on campus" even though I lived in the middle of the city, but not on campus as in Århus or DTU since Uppsala University is spread out like UCPH but to a lesser degree since Uppsala is a smaller city.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Depended on the student housing. Mine (Klostergatan) had a small private kitchen in the room and a larger common kitchen on the ground floor. In Sweden there are NO meal plans and no cheap student canteen eat outs like at lot of other European countries - the cheapest are at the nations, but I just cooked myself.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: They'll charge you for 2 full hours of cleaning even though you've spent a whole day cleaning plus charging you for damages that were there before you arrived (someone had peed on the lower bottom mattress but since there was a thinner mattress on top I didn't check during my stay...). Therefore do not expect to get your full deposit back. The good news is that there is a de facto housing guarantee. Every student that applies for housing will get it so that is a major pro compared to most other exchange destinations that you don't have to fight for housing and risking your deposit to some private landlord. Also keep in mind that other student housings than Klostergatan are outside the city center. Also they charge insane fees if you lock yourself outside your room so don't forget your key! Swedish houses are built to withstand the cold so don't be afraid of being cold indoor, but also take into account that it is quite hot indoors as well on the 5th floor during summer without air-condition since the houses are built for retaining heat.

questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted and that seemed to be the case for everyone. There were more spots than students in all my courses so no full classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You'll get what you pick so no stress about that but on the downside they really don't offer a lot of courses for statskundskabs student from UCPH unlike Sciences Po Paris (my previous Erasmus exchange).

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Approximately around the same level as UCPH (that is quite good) and also similar in the focus on the theories but not as good as Sciences Po Paris that was a lot more practical (I prefer more practical so I'm biased).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A lot more reading whole books, doing written book review assignments and seminar discussions of those read books so you can't just skip the readings the same way as you can at UCPH. A lot smaller classes than UCPH (2 classes of between 15-20) and 1 larger class with around 25-30 students. Seminars being even smaller with 8-15 students (half the class). A lot more resources per student compared to UCPH and the teachers always give quite thorough feedback during all your hand-ins and even after you get your final grade compared to UCPH where you just get a grade. Be aware that some courses only have very limited classes/lectures and require mostly readings or independent research. Also the exams are usually spread out where the book reviews, seminars, participation all count towards to final grade. Also the courses are one after the other with no overlapping courses (this being quite unique and a reason I chose Uppsala to try it). There deadlines are also more flexible (you can ask the teacher for extensions) and the grading is also just 3 possibilities: failed, passed and passed with distinction. Also if you have special needs you can even ask for a difference style of examination such as oral exams which I did instead of the normal one for 2 of the courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Comparative Politics 15 ECTS, Negotiation and Mediation in Practice 7,5 ECTS, Causes of Peace 7,5 ECTS

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Negotiation and Mediation in Practice: if you like a very practical approach, a lot of teaching hours which I loved instead of just reading but also with a huge workload for only 7,5 ECTS. The workload was equal to or greater than Comparative Politics 15 ECTS. The teacher Isak was also a brilliant teacher.
The other 2 courses were also OK, Causes of Peace was a personal choice since I'm a pacifist and Comparative Politics had some interesting perspectives of European History and Chinese politics so not a lot of overlap with DAK1+2 (I had DAK3 at Sciences Po Paris) or Comparative Politics at Sciences Po Paris.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Moving out fees of 1650 SEK...

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
There was no cheap public transport for short distances so I just walked everywhere. I wished they had Swapfiets like in Paris but no. Some students bought a bike 2nd hand on Whatsapp groups. Supermarkets in the city center are more expensive so I walked to Lidl which was cheapest but also checked etilbudsavis for discount on eggs (there are eggs for 2 SEK/egg every other week at some supermarket). Fresh fruit and vegetables are way more expensive except bananas, onions, potatoes and oranges when on discount. All other food items are cheaper than Denmark especially chocolate, nuts, milk and fil (Swedish yoghurt, but much better than yoghurt!). In total I've probably spent 20 % less on groceries (around 1500 DKK per month when buying the cheapest food in Lidl and eggs for 2 SEK/egg) than in Copenhagen. Normal people would probably spend 2000-2500 DKK in Lidl if not always eating the cheapest and if buying from the nearest ICA city probably have to spend 3000-4000 DKK for the same goods as the 2000-2500 DKK in Lidl. Like in Paris the ICA city (nearest supermarket) is equivalent to Carrefour city and unlike in Denmark where a Lidl or Netto in the city center has the same prices as those in the countryside/suburbs, in Uppsala and Paris they are around 50 % more expensive than Lidl. So if I bought the same groceries as I did in Lidl in the local ICA city nearby for convenience I would have spent MORE than back home in Copenhagen. Systembolaget is more expensive than Danish alcohol. A lot of the Uppsala museums are free for Uppsala University students! I didn't eat out a lot but the prices were quite cheaper than in Copenhagen. Clothes, glasses, eye laser operations, dentists and fish oil are a lot cheaper than in Denmark so I e.g. bought a lot of clothes from H&M and Alewalds, but also check the numerous 2nd hand shops. Also remember to join Mecenat where you'll have access to all the discounts which are way more comprehensive and numerous compared to Copenhagen's student discounts. Especially join Lidl's student discount through Mecenat. Also join the different supermarket's memberships for free such as Lidl Plus, ICA and Hemköp for weekly member discounts. Buy your scent free 1L hand soap refill from Normal. You can use your Danish phone plan in Sweden even though it is for 5 months (I didn't encounter any issues from Telmore) (the price of 200 DKK is thus the price of my Danish phone plan from back home. Internet (no WiFi in the rooms, only ethernet cable port), water, heating, electricity, waste disposal are all included in the rent. Notice that not all books are provided for free by Uppsala University, but if you search on Google or ask some of the other students you'll probably be able to get the PDF from them or else borrow the book for free from the library if you plan ahead. But if you don't do that you'll most probably have to budget some hundred DKK for buying books for each course. Uppsala University has a free comprehensive health insurance that has you covered on top the EU health insurance card so you won't need to buy a separate health insurance even including stuff like emergency dental care.
https://www.uu.se/en/study/exchange-studies/living-in-sweden/insurance

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Most were organized by the nations but there where also an international social club at the Department of Government. If you come during the Spring Semester "Valborg" is the greatest celebration and highly recommended. Join the Buddy program.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Ask someone in your housing or join a nation or join a club at your department. One could also take free Swedish lessons offered by Uppsala University at 7,5 ECTS (that don't count as ECTS points at UCPH since UCPH doesn't acknowledge language courses as valid MA courses for statskundskab). Join the Buddy program. Join the hiking group on Whatsapp that does hiking once in a while. Watch Northern lights from your Northwards facing window or go to nearby Gamla Uppsala to watch it (remember to install an Aurora app for monitering+alterting you when there are high chances for Northern lights).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Take the train up north to Lapland, Kiruna or Narvik in Norway (the final station) to e.g. see Northern lights. Or take a day trip skiing (quite cheap). Or take a day trip to Stockholm (cheap). Or take a day trip to Åland (quite cheap). Or visit some of the free museums/gardens/greenhouse/orangery. Also if you're a nationalistic Dane go to Uppsala Cathedral to see Margrete I's red silk dress that the Swedes stole from Roskilde Cathedral...

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. The Swedes were more quiet and introverted than the Danes. Less drinking. Also Swedes just walk across the road even if the light is red if there are no cars (but not as blunt as the French that totally disregard traffic lights).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to students from your courses and ask them about any events they know about.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Swedes eat so much (ultra)processed food such as ready to eat frozen dishes e.g. meatballs. Less cycling and more cars. The Swedes apparently love old USA muscle cars that pollute and are noisy. The Swedish superior-ness about their way of life, democracy, human rights, that they know how to solve other countries problems. Also the shootings and violent crime in general even though I FELT a lot more safe than in Paris. Just don't be unlucky I guess since Sweden I think is the number 1 of shootings/killings per capita in Europe besides wartime Ukraine+Russia. One day when I was in the city 3 people where killed in a hairdresser which I walked by every week on my way to and from Lidl... This shooting even appeared in Danish news:
https://nyheder.tv2.dk/live/udland/2025-04-29-tre-draebt-i-skyderi-i-svensk-by
https://www.dr.dk/nyheder/udland/tre-personer-draebt-efter-brutal-voldshandling-i-stor-svensk

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Swedes are very open to foreign cultures and they feel a bit more open to the world than Danes. In general just nice people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. UCPH only has 1 exchange spot at Uppsala University so you're going alone as I did which can be quite lonely if you're depressed and don't have energy for socializing. If possible choose a housing that doesn't have private kitchens but shared ones even though they aren't in the city center since you'll always have people to talk to then when you are at home.
2. Don't stress over housing or courses, you'll get them.
3. Don't come here to drink alcohol but to appreciate the low population density and lots of nature.
4. Appreciate a quite different way of teaching.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
You don't need cash. I recommend using Revolut for 7500 DKK free exchange to SEK each month. Remember to buy your train tickets to and from Uppsala as early as possible for the cheapest price (become a SJ member helps since they regularly send you newsletters with time limited discounts such as extra points or 20 % off all journeys in a time period so remember to become a member some months in advance) but also remember that you only can get student discounts on the way back since you don't have a Mecenat card yet on the way up. Uppsala isn't a place to wear fancy or business clothes and has a more outdoor-ish vibe in stark contrast to Paris. Remember to bring your warmest outdoor clothes for the long winter period, where Spring arrives at least a month later than in Copenhagen and you can still experience nights with negative temperatures in April/May. Check Weatherspark:
https://weatherspark.com/compare/y/74001~82852/Comparison-of-the-Average-Weather-in-Copenhagen-and-Uppsala

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning to cook and feed myself, to go on a hermit-ish slow retreat for mental cleansing and detoxing myself from all the dopamine addicting activities and in general high speed in Copenhagen where there is always something to do (FOMO). Quite comparable as to going to your summer house in Denmark for ½ a year. Appreciating the grandness of nature and the earth with the Northern lights every once in a while and feeling tiny compared to Copenhagen where there are people everywhere. My favorite activity of watching from my 5th floor (highest floor), Northward facing window with no other tall buildings blocking the view, watching the street life, the suns movement across the sky, Northern lights, birds, and when reaching summer the sky that nearly doesn't darken because Uppsala is so close to the polar circle. Appreciating that humans can survive in such cold, dark and much more hostile environment compared to Copenhagen and even built Universities and live their whole lives here which requires quite some resilience with winter temperatures going below -10 degrees celsius with wind chill on top.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Loneliness and I missed human touch (but I was also quite depressed so I didn't have the energy to go out and socialize and having private kitchens at Klostergatan also removed the social aspect of shared kitchens, therefore if possible don't choose Klostergatan but one of the housings with shared kitchens e.g. on the same floor). Craving fresh fruits and vegetables.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Good luck, I'm sure you'll have a better experience than me. In total I personally preferred Sciences Po Paris over Uppsala, but they are very, very different exchanges, one could say polar opposites.

questions.answer: Yes
